items.question: What is a C# delegate, and how do Func and Action differ from a custom delegate type?
items.answer: A delegate is a sealed CLR type that stores a method reference (and optionally a target object) whose parameter list and return type are compatible. Instantiating it binds a method group; invoking it calls that method. Func and Action are generic BCL aliases for the common shapes. Custom delegates still matter when the type name is the contract — especially events — or when you need ref/out parameters that older Func overloads did not express cleanly.
followUps: Does the delegate signature include the return type?
What does variance allow when assigning methods to delegates?
items.sixtySeconds: Typed method pointer plus optional target. Func returns; Action is void. Custom type when the name is the API.

items.question: How does multicast invocation work, and what goes wrong if a handler throws?
items.answer: Combining delegates with + or += produces a multicast delegate. Raise walks the invocation list in subscription order, synchronously. If one handler throws, later handlers do not run unless you call GetInvocationList() and invoke each entry in a try/catch. That is the interview answer for a RabbitMQ fan-out that must still ack after a metrics handler fails.
followUps: How do you remove one handler without clearing the whole list?
items.sixtySeconds: Invocation list, left to right. One exception aborts the rest unless you iterate GetInvocationList yourself.

items.question: Why is event safer than a public delegate field on a long-lived consumer?
items.answer: A public delegate field lets any caller assign null, replace the list, or invoke it. event exposes only add and remove (+= and -=). The publisher still decides when to raise. On an SQS hosted service that lives for days, a short-lived pipeline that += a handler and forgets -= keeps that pipeline graph reachable from the host. Unsubscribe in Dispose, or do not use instance events for process-wide buses.
followUps: When would you implement custom add/remove accessors?
items.sixtySeconds: event = add/remove only. Public field = anyone can wipe or fire. Leaks = publisher holds subscriber.

items.question: When do you pick a local function over a lambda?
items.answer: Local functions are named, can be recursive without a dummy assignment, can use yield return, can apply attributes, and are not converted to a delegate unless you pass them as one. Argument validation before an iterator or async body lives in the outer method; the local function holds the iterator. Lambdas always allocate a delegate (and often a closure class). static on either forbids capture.
followUps: Can a lambda contain yield return?
How does a static local function interact with captured variables?
items.sixtySeconds: Local function: named, yield, cheaper if not turned into a delegate. Lambda: inline callback for LINQ and events.

items.question: What did C# 14 add to extensions compared with this-parameter methods?
items.answer: Classic extensions are static methods with a this receiver, instance-only, methods-only. C# 14 extension blocks inside a static class declare instance members (methods, properties) and a second form with a type-only receiver for static methods, static properties, and operators. Both compile to static methods in IL. They never override real instance members. Interviewers want you to say properties and static extensions are new, not that this-methods vanished.
followUps: Can an extension property replace an instance property of the same name?
How do ref receivers work on structs?
items.sixtySeconds: C# 14: extension { } blocks, properties, static type members. Still lose to real members. this-methods still legal.
